node.label: Doreen Massey
node.date_label: Spatial Divisions of Labour (1984; second edition 1995) · Space, Place and Gender (1994) · For Space (2005)
node.description: Space, Place and Gender (1994) argues that space is the product of intersecting social relations and relates the conceptualization of space and place to the social construction of gender relations. For Space (2005) develops this relational account: different histories coexist in space, whose continuing construction keeps political possibilities open. This approach makes places encounters between trajectories rather than self-contained identities. In “A Global Sense of Place” (1991; collected in Space, Place and Gender, 1994) and “Power-geometry and a progressive sense of place” (1993), she develops an account of places shaped by wider connections and unequal relations of power. Its political implications remained disputed. In the 2007 review symposium, as Massey’s reply records, Matt Sparke raised questions about responsibility and the truth status of her spatial claims. She agreed that relational thinking does not guarantee a particular political response. Her own interventions include a feminist criticism of Harvey in “Flexible Sexism” (1991) and the coauthored dialogue “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), with Stuart Hall.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Spatial Divisions of Labour (1984; second edition 1995); “Flexible Sexism” (1991); “Politics and Space/Time” (1992); Space, Place and Gender (1994); For Space (2005); “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), with Stuart Hall.
node.scope_note: Selected publisher samples of For Space and public opening paragraphs of Space, Place and Gender read; neither book read in full. Politics and Space/Time and Flexible Sexism read only in public openings. Interpreting the crisis read selectively through p. 67. The complete 2007 author response was read; reviewers’ original contributions and the criticized monographs remain unread. Places and Their Pasts could not be freshly accessed. The added account of the 1991 and 1993 essays uses selected pages of Roger Lee’s 2018 memoir, the 1994 collection’s contents and Cambridge’s public opening of the 1993 essay; neither essay was read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hall and Massey coauthor the dialogue “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), examining the financial crisis through conjunctural analysis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher PDF p. 57 credits both authors and labels their turns; selected pp. 57–67 read. Coauthorship only; Hall’s particular formulations are not assigned wholesale to Massey.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), Massey says rereading Althusser helps her understand the crisis as a conjunction of economic, political and philosophical processes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: p. 59, Doreen’s turn: “looked at the Prison Notebooks, and Althusser”. Lee pp. 164, 167 corroborates an earlier debt to overdetermination. Althusser originals unread; no sole derivation asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Interpreting the crisis” (2010), Massey uses her rereading of Gramsci’s Prison Notebooks to argue against an exclusively economic account of crisis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: p. 59, same explicitly labelled Doreen turn: “don’t only ‘do the economy’”. Hall identifies Gramsci on pp. 58–59; no independent Notebooks reading claimed. Her use is distinct from Hall’s exposition.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Flexible Sexism” (1991), Massey criticizes Harvey’s The Condition of Postmodernity (1989) for excluding feminist contributions from geography’s modernism–postmodernism debate.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2018 Reader reprint, introduction, last two displayed paragraphs: “denial” of feminism; Cambridge chapter 15, pp. 221–242, opening only. Original pp. 31–57 remainder unread. Joint criticism also names Soja. Distinct from existing edge_1518 about tradition and place in 1995.

proposed_edges.relationship: Massey uses Lefebvre’s warning about undefined spatial concepts to frame “Politics and Space/Time” (1992).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Public opening, paragraph beginning Buried in these unacknowledged disagreements; names The Production of Space and endorses its demand to debate spatial meanings. For Space sample p. 17 repeats this starting point. Limited framing debt, not adoption of Lefebvre’s whole theory; originals and subscription remainder unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: For Space (2005) argues that de Certeau’s tactics–strategy distinction reinforces the space–time dualism his account seeks to escape.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample pp. 25–27, especially p. 26: “cements into place”; references de Certeau’s 1984 English edition. Original unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: For Space (2005) criticizes Giddens and Beck’s risk-society writing for opposing dynamic culture to stable nature.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample p. 160: “such dualisms”; joint attribution followed by Nigel Clark’s 2002 argument. Chapter 9 and Giddens originals unread; limited joint criticism.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions stable nature in risk theory

proposed_edges.relationship: Space, Place and Gender (1994) develops a wider notion of spatiality as the product of intersecting social relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: JSTOR part I introduction, displayed p. 19 opening: “spatial fetishism”. Only opening read; theoretical contribution, not a claim about reception or the whole discipline.

proposed_edges.relationship: Space, Place and Gender (1994) relates the conceptualization of space and place to the social construction of gender relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: JSTOR part III introduction, displayed p. 177 opening: “construction of the other”. A theoretical resource for gender history; historical uptake by particular historians is not established. Full section unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: For Space (2005) treats places as encounters between trajectories with different histories, making belonging open to renegotiation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample pp. 149–151, Hamburg boulder example: “constellation of trajectories”. Historical-geographical framework, not evidence of adoption by a historian.

proposed_edges.relationship: Massey’s For Space (2005) supplied an open-ended account of place that Alan Lester used in imperial-colonial history, as Indra Sengupta explains in her introduction to Memory, History, and Colonialism (2009).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Sengupta’s discussion on printed pp. 7–8 and notes 19–22 in the institute’s own publication. The body explicitly attributes Lester’s account of places as intersections of trajectories to Massey, then explains its usefulness for understanding colonial and postcolonial sites of memory. This supports a bounded contribution to imperial-colonial historiography. Lester has no eligible endpoint in the supplied lists, so no person edge is proposed. Neither For Space nor Lester’s original article was read for this proposal.

proposed_edges.relationship: Massey’s Spatial Divisions of Labour (1984) supplies an account of domestic economic geography within the international division of labour that Lachlan MacKinnon and Steven High use to frame Canadian deindustrialization in “Deindustrialization in Canada: New Perspectives” (2023).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s own open article, especially its discussion of uneven deindustrialization and international industrial restructuring, and note 19. The authors invoke Massey by name in the body, quote her argument, and immediately discuss its consequences for Canadian manufacturing workers. Note 19 identifies the 1984 book, although it renders Divisions in the singular. This is evidence of use within labour historiography, not a claim that Massey founded the field. MacKinnon and High have no eligible endpoints in the supplied lists. The underlying Massey book was not read for this proposal.
proposed_edges.map_label: International divisions of labour and industrial decline
